title: Hannah spoke up (Berakhot 31b)
hookLine: the Talmud praises how boldly Hannah reasoned with God
tomorrow: God says 'let Me alone.' what does Moses do?

cards: Some people send the food back when it's wrong, email the professor about the grade, ask the nurse one more time. It's awkward, and it often works. The Talmud says Hannah prayed like that.
Quiet voice, yes. Timid words, no. Rabbi Elazar says she spoke boldly toward heaven.
So yes: you can argue with God and still be praying.

teach.b: Listen to how she opens, in Samuel: "O LORD of hosts, if thou wilt indeed look on the affliction of thine handmaid." The Talmud stops on that name, LORD of hosts.
Rabbi Elazar says that from the day God created the world, no one had called God "hosts" until Hannah did.

teach.h: NO ONE HAD SAID IT BEFORE HER.
teach.b: Then it imagines why she chose it. Master of the world, of all the hosts upon hosts You've made, is it hard for You to give me one son? And it adds a parable.

teach.h: THE POOR MAN AT THE FEAST.
teach.b: A king makes a feast for his servants. A poor man stands at the door asking for one piece of bread, and no one notices him.
So he pushes through to the king and says: my lord king, out of this whole feast, is one piece hard for you to give? That's Hannah's prayer. Not loud, but not small.
She makes her case. Here's what to tell a friend tonight.
The same tractate that learns quiet prayer from Hannah's lips learns boldness from her words, and praises her for both.
One way to hear it: you only argue with someone you believe is listening.

how: Jewish prayer makes room for bold requests and honest complaint, from the psalms to the personal words some add to the Amidah; Hannah's prayer is read in synagogue on the first day of Rosh Hashanah.

o: Hannah led the prayers at Shiloh in Eli's place
Hannah made her case to God plainly and boldly
Hannah raised her voice so the whole sanctuary heard

p: first said by Hannah, says Rabbi Elazar
is one son hard to give?
the poor man at the feast
is one piece hard for you?

s: in Jewish prayer, arguing with God is disrespectful
the Talmud praises how Hannah reasoned with God.
the Talmud says no one called God 'LORD of hosts' before Hannah
Rabbi Elazar: from the day God created the world, until Hannah.
Hannah's boldness meant she prayed loudly
her voice wasn't heard; the boldness was in her words.

games.q: your sister needs a recommendation letter and is scared to ask her busy coach. what would Hannah's way look like?
o: ask plainly, with her reason: out of everything you do, is one letter hard?
wait quietly and hope the coach offers one without being asked.
demand it loudly in front of the whole team so it can't be refused.
games.why: Hannah's prayer, as the Talmud hears it, is the poor man at the feast: is one piece hard for you to give? plain, reasoned, and not loud.

practice: Write one bold sentence: something you want for someone you love, said plainly, with your reason, the way Hannah made her case. Leave out the softeners, the maybes and the if-it's-not-too-much. Read it back once, quietly.

wordCard.voice: Hannah spoke up. The Talmud praises how she reasoned with God: of all Your hosts, is one son hard to give?

orig.note: Hebrew: hosts. the Talmud says Hannah was the first to call God by it.

carryVoice: Your line: Hannah spoke up. A quiet voice can carry a bold case. Twenty-three of fifty.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 31b (Rabbi Elazar on Hannah's bold words; Hannah first calls God 'hosts'; the parable of the poor man at the king's feast)
